newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Asia still capital magnet, but Latam growing - BIS.
newsitem.headline: Asia still capital magnet, but Latam growing - BIS.

text.p: Asia is still the main magnet for capital from industrialised countries, but new lending to Latin America and Eastern Europe accelerated sharply in the second half of 1996, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said.
European banks also strengthened their hold on international bank lending, but BIS noted North American banks were expanding further with a strong upsurge in credits to Russia.

New lending by banks in industrial nations to Latin America, the Middle East, Africa, Asia and Eastern Europe set a new record of $77.8 billion in the second half of last year with outstanding claims rising to $993.1 billion at the end of 1996.

BIS said in its latest semi-annual report on international bank lending that the record bank activity seemed to be little affected by the growing popularity of stocks and bonds from emerging markets, strains in some countries' banking systems, large current account deficits or widespread attempts to limit reliance on volatile short-term capital flows.
"Ample world liquidity and slowing or weak corporate demand for funds in the industrialised world continued to encourage banking flows to a broad range of countries," said BIS.
Banking flows to emerging countries was also on the rise as the so-called Tequila effect in the wake of the Mexican financial crises in late 1994 continued to fade.
The figures reflect new international lending by banks that report to BIS, bank to the world's central banks.

BIS reporting banks come from the Group of 10 (G10) leading industrial nations plus Austria, Denmark, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg, Norway and Spain. G10 originally comprised the U.S., Japan, Canada, Germany, Britain, France, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden and now includes an 11th member, Switzerland.

In spite of growing caution by lenders towards certain countries, BIS said lending to Asia rose by $31.3 billion with Korean borrowers the most active, followed by Indonesia, China, the Philippines and Malaysia.
"High domestic interest rates and sustained strong economic growth in Indonesia, the Philippines and Malaysia continued to act as a magnet for banking funds," BIS said.
In contrast, financing to Thailand started to dry up, only rising $1.9 billion in the second half of last year compared with $8.0 billion in the first half of the year.
Lending to Latin America accelerated by $23.2 billion after stagnant or modest activity in recent years.
Argentina, whose economy and local financial system is recovering, was the main beneficiary with lending up $5.5 billion, ahead of Brazil, Colombia and Mexico.
BIS said the revival of lending to Colombia, up $4.7 billion, was particularly striking given the country's recent economic weakness and that it traditionally is not a major borrower.
In Eastern Europe, tight monetary policies and reduced inflationary pressures lead to a record $13 billion inflow.
The upsurge was most pronounced for Russia, where lending rose $5.6 billion, but there was also a strong $3.4 billion rise vis-a-vis Hungary.
Russia's public sector was the principal recipient of funds as tight monetary policy and limited exchange rate depreciation enhanced foreigners' appetite for Russian Treasury paper.

European banks were once again the most active group of international lenders and now hold 54 percent of total claims of $993.1 billion compared with 17 percent by Japanese banks and 15 percent by North American banks.
While European banks have traditionally played a dominant role in Eastern Europe, their lead in Asia is more recent.
By the end of 1996, European banks accounted for 42 percent of all claims on Asia compared with 32 percent by Japanese banks, traditionally the dominant lenders.
North American banks continued to expand, not only in their traditionally-strong area of Latin America, but also in Eastern Europe, particularly Russia, BIS said.
The funds channelled by U.S. banks are of considerably shorter-term nature than those of European banks, reflecting the demand for dollars, the main vehicle in foreign exchange deals.

But it may also reflect a different strategy used by U.S. banks, which appear to place greater emphasis on off-balance sheet business, such as securities underwriting and derivatives risk management services rather than traditional lending.
